issues.legal_issue: An acquisition notification may be allowed to remain despite non-compliance with statutory preconditions when the circumstances support a conditional disposition.
material_facts: The High Court found that statutory requirements for completing the scheme had not been strictly complied with and annulled the acquisition notification.

The Supreme Court found no mala fides; the authority’s order had apparently been treated as the required resolution, and the landowners had not raised the absence of valid authority in their earlier challenge.
The land had been substantially improved under the scheme, and fresh proceedings could follow if the notification were annulled.
issues.conclusion: The appeals were allowed and the High Court’s judgment was vacated. The acquisition was allowed to remain, subject to the Court’s conditions on the notification date and compensation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and section 50(2) of the Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam, 1973, were relevant to the acquisition and scheme. Although the statutory preconditions had not been strictly met, the Court fashioned a conditional disposition in light of the absence of mala fides, the circumstances in which the defect emerged, the improvements made, and the prospect of fresh proceedings. No earlier cases are cited.

rule.if: appeal_from_acquisition_annulment and statutory_steps_incomplete and no_mala_fides_found and land_substantially_improved and defect_not_raised_earlier

predicates.appeal_from_acquisition_annulment: The acquiring body appealed a judgment that had annulled an acquisition notification.
predicates.statutory_steps_incomplete: The statutory requirements for completing the scheme connected with the acquisition had not been strictly complied with.
predicates.no_mala_fides_found: The court found no mala fides in the acquiring body’s conduct.
predicates.land_substantially_improved: The acquiring body had substantially improved the land or its surroundings under the scheme.
predicates.defect_not_raised_earlier: The landowners had not raised the defect concerning authority for the scheme in an earlier challenge.

issues.definition: When an appeal from an annulment involves incomplete statutory steps, no finding of mala fides, substantial improvements, and a defect not raised earlier, the acquisition may be retained subject to conditions.

issues.legal_issue: When an acquisition is retained after the notification date is shifted to account for delay and improvements, compensation must reflect that date while limiting the landowners’ benefit from improvements made by the acquiring body.
material_facts: The acquisition notification had been issued in 1985, and the Court directed that it be treated as issued on 1 January 1988.
During the intervening period, the acquiring body had made the bulk of the improvements in the neighbourhood, substantially increasing the land’s potential value.
issues.conclusion: The land’s market value was to be determined as of 1 January 1988. Only 25 per cent of the potential value attributable to the acquiring body’s improvements was available to the landowners, while all other legitimate valuation considerations remained applicable.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the Court directed that the notification be treated as having a later date and that market value be determined with reference to that date. It limited the landowners’ entitlement to potential value attributable to improvements made by the acquiring body during the intervening period, while preserving other legitimate valuation considerations. No earlier cases are cited.

predicates.acquisition_appeal: The case was an appeal concerning an acquisition challenged by the landowners.
predicates.authority_improved_surroundings_during_d: The acquiring body made improvements in the surroundings during the period before the notification was treated as taking effect.
predicates.land_potential_value_increased_from_thos: The land’s potential value increased because of improvements made by the acquiring body.

issues.definition: When an acquisition appeal concerns land whose potential value increased through the acquiring body’s improvements during delay, valuation uses the deemed notification date and limits the value attributable to those improvements.

issues.legal_issue: A judicially treated separate acquisition notification does not extend the enhanced-compensation benefit to owners whose lands were acquired under earlier notifications.
material_facts: The Court treated the respondents’ acquisition as having a separate notification date.
Other owners’ lands had already been acquired under earlier notifications, and the Court’s direction would otherwise have affected their ability to seek the same statutory benefit.
issues.conclusion: The Court’s direction did not extend the benefit under section 28A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, to owners whose lands had already been acquired under the earlier notifications, because the direction was to be treated as a separate notification.
issues.legal_principle: Section 28A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, was not to benefit owners whose lands had been acquired under the earlier notifications. The Court treated its direction concerning the respondents’ notification as a separate notification, not a common notification for that purpose. No earlier cases are cited.

predicates.earlier_land_acquisitions_exist: Other owners’ lands had already been acquired under earlier notifications.
predicates.court_treats_later_acquisition_as_separa: The court treated the acquisition at issue as having a separate notification rather than sharing a notification with the earlier acquisitions.

issues.definition: When earlier land acquisitions exist and the court treats the later acquisition as separate, the benefit is not extended to those earlier acquisitions.
